ANSE 2026: Promoting Electric Propulsion
        Technical Design Report:
  Pittsburgh Electric Propulsion’s Skips
    Soumik Chakraborty, Varun Patel, Chris Yeager,
   Ben Swanson, Jacob Sullivan, Rafayel Amirkhanyan

pages.text:
Pittsburgh Electric Propulsion | 3

Abstract—This report presents the design
and development strategy of Pittsburgh
Electric Propulsion's autonomous surface
vehicle (ASV) for ASNE’s Promoting Electric
Propulsion 2026 competition. As a first-year
team competing in the Autonomy challenge, we
focused on creating a system that prioritizes
safety and reliability, ensuring that all
mechanical and electrical components are
integrated into a sound system. Likewise, the
software architecture, built on ROS2 Humble
and running on an onboard Jetson Orin,
prioritizes core autonomy functionality,
notabally localization, navigation, and safe
control systems. Throughout the design and
manufacturing timeline, the ASV has been
tested, both physically in our university’s pool
and through simulated test environments
I. SYSTEM OVERVIEW

Pittsburgh Electric Propulsion's ASV
Skips is a carbon fiber displacement catamaran
designed to autonomously navigate a GPS
waypoint racecourse for ASNE's Promoting
Electric Propulsion 2026 competition. As a firstyear team, our design philosophy prioritizes safety
and reliability, above all else, building a robust
foundation for future competition seasons. The
vehicle is organized into three integrated
subsystems. The mechanical system provides a
stable, lightweight platform capable of high-speed
operation. The electrical system separates
propulsion and control into isolated 48V and 12V
voltage domains, with a layered hardware safety
circuit ensuring that any single fault is sufficient
to cut propulsion. The autonomy stack, built on
ROS2 Humble and running on a Jetson Orin AGX,
fuses GPS, IMU, and magnetometer data through
an Extended Kalman Filter to achieve reliable
localization, and uses a Line-of-Sight guidance
algorithm
to
navigate
the
racecourse
autonomously.
Throughout development, each subsystem
was validated independently before full system
integration was tested in both a Gazebo VRX
simulation environment and physically in the
university pool.

II.MECHANICAL SUBSYSTEM DESIGN
III.HULL

For the hull, we decided to go with a V-Hull
Planing boat as it provides an ideal combination of
straight-line speed and handling in rough water.
Through referencing last year’s crafts that
competed in the ASNE PEP Unmanned category,
we came up with a set of targets for our hull to
fulfil to be considered a success. The main
criterion for the hull was being able to reach a peak
theoretical speed of 30 knots while also being
stable in the rough waters. Using last year’s craft
as a guideline for our designs, we decided our
boat’s length to be in the range of 6 feet.
After that, we researched common deadrise
angles for V-Hulls. The most common deadrise
angles for handling rough water fall within the
range of 20-24°, as the deeper angles provide more
stability in rougher waters. However, with the
higher deadrise angles, it would also become
harder for the boat to reach a planing state.
Eventually, we settled on running a deadrise angle
of 22°, as that would provide stability while also
not sacrificing speed.
For the bottom of the boat, we decided to add
additional lifting strakes to make it easier for the
boat to lift itself out of the water. The lifting
strakes are an inch thick at its maximum point to
maximize the potential surface area to generate lift
but are also small enough to not have a sizeable
effect on the overall hydrodynamic structure of the
boat.
For the validation, we went with a two-step
validation cycle during the design process. The
initial designs were tested with Orca3Ds
hydrostatics and hydrodynamic analysis features,
which helped us get good estimates on whether
certain designs would be successful or not. Then,
the final designs were validated with ANSYS

Fluent with a multiphase simulation as a final
validation.
For the hydrostatic and hydrodynamic
analyses in Orca3D, we used fixed load cases to
get accurate predictions of the center of gravity of
the whole boat. These load cases mainly consisted
of the heavier components of the boat including
the motor, battery, motor controller, and so on, as
those were the main contributors to the center of
gravity which was then used in analyses. Overall,
the total weight of everything in the boat was
calculated to be 66 kgs, which was then used
subsequently in the analyses.
The final design yielded the following static
stability graph at free float conditions with
Orca3D’s hydrostatics report:

The maximum righting angle of the hull
ended up being roughly 80 mm at a 45-degree heel
angle, showing the correction ability of the craft
when pushed to the higher heel angles.
Additionally, the trim angle remains close to the
zero-trim axis until a heel angle of roughly 20
degrees, after which the trim also starts to tilt,
though not at a concerning rate. The trim angle
does not change much with the heel angle,
especially when the heel angle is under 45
degrees, which is the expected maximum heel
angle that the craft should face.
After the hydrostatics validation that the
hull will be able to survive the rough waters, we
run a hydrodynamics validation using Orca3D’s
Planing Analysis to ensure that our craft will be

able to reach our desired velocity. With this
analysis, we are mainly looking at whether our
motor, which can supply 12 kW of continuous
power, can power our boat to the necessary speed
of 30 knots.
For the planing analysis, we took the
resistive design margin to be 30% to account for
the worst possible scenario in all aspects of
manufacturing. Additionally, we used a
propulsive efficiency of 80% as an additional
buffer as this was our first time designing an
outboard, and hence we were unsure about our
overall propulsive efficiency with our powertrain.
After taking everything into account, the
final design yielded the following power-speed
graph using Orca3D’s Planing Analysis:

As our motors maximum continuous
power output is 12 kW, that translates to a
maximum speed of just over 33 knots, which
exceeds our initial expectations regarding the
overall speed of the craft.
After this, we validated the final design
with ANSYS Fluent Multiphase simulation to
ensure that the boat matches the same trim angle
as was given in the analysis. The simulation
provided us with data that closely matched with
the one provided by Orca3D’s Planing Analysis,
which confirmed our boat design and its stability.
The finalized hull design is as follows,
with the overall dimensions being 72 in x 24 in x
14 in.

vacuum bagging to ensure the epoxy was coated
evenly over the entire surface.
We also used a similar process for
manufacturing the lid, however for that we used a
cut wooden board as our mold as it was a flat
surface and did not require many intricacies.
In regard to manufacturing the hull, we
opted to make the hull out of carbon fiber due to
its high strength to weight ratio. To manufacture
carbon fiber, we used a positive mold
manufactured using a combination of 3D printing
and foam, which we then laid up with carbon fiber
which was then vacuum bagged.
For the mold, we used a combination of
ELFOAM P300 and 3D printing to make the
mold, as the foam was only able to create the mold
for the first 10 inches of the hull’s depth as that
was all the foam we were able to procure. For the
remaining 4 inches of the hull depth, we 3D
printed the mold using PLA on our Prusa XL and
Bambu P1S.
For the foam, we were able to glue the
sheets of foam together using West System’s 105
Epoxy Resin mixed with their 206 Slow Hardener.
After gluing the sheets together, we were then able
to route the foam at the CNC Lathe at our
university machine shop. With the 3D prints, we
glued them together using superglue and then used
the Epoxy Resin to glue the foam to the prints.
After assembling the mold, we applied
Bondo to fill in all of the gaps to make the surface
smooth, after which we applied a layer of
Fiberglast’s Orange Tooling Gelcoat to seal the
mold and make sure none of the foam or 3D prints
seep into the carbon. Finally, we applied a layer of
TR 104 Mold Release to allow us to properly
remove the finished carbon fiber.
Once the mold was prepared, we laid up
the carbon fiber using the Epoxy Resin and used

Within the finished hull, we put custom
ribs made from MDF to prevent buckling from
sideways forces due to waves. The ribs also served
another vital purpose, as it allowed us to mount an
acrylic sheet to the ribs upon which all of the
enclosures sat upon. Additionally, the lid screwed
into the top of the ribs using threaded inserts that
were inserted into the wood.
A. Outboard
For our motor, we are using an ME 1117 to power
our boat. We planned on the motor to be mounted
in an outboard configuration to increase the power
to performance of the overall craft. Additionally,
it makes it significantly easier for the software as
turning the outboard has a direct correlation to the
amount the boat turns unlike a rudder where the
correlation has be carefully tested and studied.
We planned on manufacturing our own outboard
using OshCut to bend most of our materials for the
exterior of the outboard and used McMaster to buy
most of our gearing and propulsion system
components.
For the propulsion system, we attached a keyed
shaft to the motor, which was then connected to
two bevel gears at right angles, which then drive a
propeller. The entire propulsion system has
bearings and dampers at places to mitigate the
effect of vibration or external forces onto the
propulsion system.
With the outside shell, we used a lot of bent metal
from OshCut due to their convenience and speed
of shipping, which allowed us to quickly assembly
everything shortly after design.

The bent metal for creating the main body was
then mounted to a motor mount using custom
angled brackets. The motor mount itself also has a
protrusion where the push rod connects on to. The
push rod is then connected to a servo that sits
inside the boat which controls the direction of
travel. On the outside, we attached a tapered
bellow to ensure no water seeps in with the hole
made
for
the
push
rod.

Near the bottom of the outboard, we
mounted cavitation plates to reduce the effect of
cavitation from the propeller and therefore
increase efficiency. The shell for the lower unit
was resin 3D printed to ensure high resolution and
strength in the high-pressure environment.
The cover for the motor also has holes to
allow the wires from the motor controller. Which
is sitting within the boat, to be wired to the motor,

which is outside the boat on the outboard. The
holes are covered with O-Rings to mitigate the
water entry during operation.
The outboard is then mounted to the boat using a
clevis bracket which is attached to the motor
mount. The clevis bracket allows the outboard to
rotate freely while also ensuring that it does not
break off while running.
B. Enclosures
For the internal enclosures, we divided the
enclosures into Software and Electrical
Enclosures. These two enclosures will sit near
opposite sides of the boat but will host different
components for different purposes.
Within the Software Enclosure, the Jetson Orin,
12 V battery and Low Voltage (12V) PCB are
mounted. The Jetson is the central computer for
the craft, and it is therefore essential that it does
not overheat. To counteract this, we added
mounting holes to mount cooling fans onto the
software enclosure in case the temperatures of the
Jetson start to increase dramatically. The fans have
been mounted such that they are easily removable
in case the Jetson is well below a concerning
temperature, which is helpful as it would extend
the battery life of the 12 V battery.
For the Electrical Enclosure, we decided to mount
the battery, BMS and Safety Circuit PCB. In
regard to the battery, however, no battery on the
market was available that fits our specifications
with weight and power capacity, and so we
decided to design and manufacture our own.
With the battery, we designed custom cell mounts
for the Molicell 21700 cells that we used, and we
connected the cells with nickel strips. The cell
holders were 3D printed with Polycarbonate due
to its high temperature resistance. The cells were
then housed in a module, which was then mounted
within the electrical enclosure.
D. Mechanical Risks and Mitigation
One of the biggest risks of an electric boat
is preventing the leakage of water into the boat,
especially into any important electrical system. To
combat this, we made sure that all high voltage
systems are covered with at least two layers of
waterproofing to at least IPX4, which are then

pages.text:
Pittsburgh Electric Propulsion | 7

thoroughly tested before being put into the boat.
To test the enclosures and overall waterproofing
of the boat, we first spray it with a hose and
monitor any potential water leakage. After that,
we dump water in a controlled manner using
buckets to recreate a worst-case scenario of the
boat potentially sinking, and only if the enclosures
remain dry internally after those tests will it be
allowed on the boat.
Another risk is the hull potentially sinking
with all the important components. To test this, we
first test the bare hull in a pool and model all of
the internal components using spare dumbbells
which closely matched the weights of all the
components within the boat. Once the boat passes
that, we add extra weights to monitor when the
boat starts to sink to a dangerous level and monitor
that weight. Only after the hull passes the basic
floatation test do we put any electrical components
into the boat.
During manufacturing, one of the major
concerns we had was whether the routing failed or
if a printed part did not hold up to the standards
we set. To mitigate this problem, we worked
closely with other student clubs on campus to
potentially use their resources if any of ours failed
such as potentially using some leftover foam from
our FSAE team.
Another huge area of risk is if a designed
component fails due to poor design. To mitigate
this, the Mechanical team meets multiple times a
week to go over designs so that everyone can help
each other and give each other constructive
criticism. Additionally, we utilize simulation tools
such as ANSYS Structural and Fluent to ensure
that our components behave as calculated.
III. ELECTRICAL SYSTEM DESIGN
A. Research & Background

Our electrical system focuses on three
main areas: propulsion and motion control,
battery and power management, and safety.
Before beginning design work, we set an
initial goal of our ASV travelling 30 knots, aimed
at 15 horsepower. Designed our system around
this, spec'ing out the MotoEnergy ME1117 motor
for use with a Sevcon Gen 4 motor controller.
This goal, in addition to our choice of outboard

control, was the driving factor in the decision to
create our own 48V battery.
Above all, we prioritized creating a safe
and reliable system, on power management,
emergency stops, and hardware safety limits.
Thus, extensive research was done by
researching sealing marine electrical systems and
ensuring isolation in case of an incident.
B. System Design

The electrical system is divided into two
isolated voltage domains: a 12 V low-voltage
(LV) system responsible for all onboard
computing, sensing, and safety control, and a 48
V high-voltage (HV) system dedicated
exclusively to propulsion. This separation
ensures that transients and switching noise on the
high-current propulsion bus cannot propagate to
sensitive navigation hardware, and simplifies safe
isolation of the drivetrain during testing and
maintenance.
The LV system is sourced from a
commercially procured 12 V battery and
distributed through a custom low-voltage
distribution board. This board powers the Jetson
Orin AGX, which serves as the primary onboard
compute platform, as well as the ICM-45605
IMU and MMC5983MA magnetometer, both of
which share a common I²C bus, feeding inertial
and heading data to the autonomy stack. An
ESP32 with an onboard LoRa module handles
decoding of SBUS signals from the RC receiver
and provides a long-range telemetry and override
link. GPS positioning is provided by a SparkFun
ZED-F9P RTK GPS module connected to the
Jetson via USB-C.

main areas: propulsion and motion control,
battery and power management, and safety.

initial goal of our ASV travelling 30 knots, aimed

For power management, a buck-boost
converter on the LV board provides regulated
power supplies to the Jetson, ensuring it is isolated
from both batteries and maintaining a safe, smooth
current draw. There is only one bridge between the
LV and HV systems, being the CAN bus between
the Jetson and the Sevcon controller. However, we
ensured to use an isolated CAN transceiver (with
separate ground pours in our PCBs) to bridge this
communication safely, preserving isolation
between the two systems.
The HV propulsion system consists of a
Motenergy ME 1117 brushless DC motor driven
by a Sevcon Gen4 Size 2 motor controller. The
ME 1117 was selected for its efficiency profile in
our target operating range and its compatibility
with field-oriented control. The 48 V battery pack
was manufactured in-house and is managed by an
Orion BMS, which continuously monitors
individual cell voltages, state of charge, pack
temperature, and current draw, providing both
data to the autonomy stack and a hardware
interlock into the safety circuit.

and disconnects the HV propulsion bus. The

produced the expected motor response before the

The 48 V battery pack was assembled inhouse with attention to cell-level fusing, secure
mechanical retention, and environmental sealing.
Following assembly, the pack was tested to verify
cell balance, BMS communication, and contactor
operation under load. Safety circuit behavior was
validated by triggering each input independently
(E-stop, BMS fault, Sevcon fault, and software
command) and confirming that each reliably
opened the contactor.

All electronics are housed in sealed,
waterproof enclosures suited to marine operation.
Deutsch connectors are used throughout the
wiring harness for their resistance to vibration,
moisture, and repeated mating cycles. Shielded
cables are used on the motor encoder and CAN
bus lines, with shields grounded at a single point
to reject radiated interference from the motor and
the Sevcon's switching waveforms without
introducing ground loops.
D. Electrical Risks and Mitigation

Motor Fault - If the software loses the ability to
command the motor, whether due to a CAN bus
fault, a Sevcon internal fault, or a broader software
failure, the motor could potentially continue
running at its last commanded torque. To prevent
this at the hardware level, we wired the Sevcon
fault output directly into the safety circuit,
ensuring the contactor opens and propulsion is cut
regardless of whether the software is working as
intended. The system also polls the drive's fault
log on startup and will not enable the motor if preexisting faults are detected.
Battery Fault - A fault within the battery pack
(such as a cell overvoltage, undervoltage,
overcurrent, or overtemperature condition) poses
a risk of pack damage or, in the worst case,
thermal runaway, posing a risk to everyone
involved. The Orion BMS continuously monitors

all cells and enforces hard protection thresholds in
hardware, opening the main contactor
immediately if any limit is exceeded. This
interlock operates independently of the autonomy
stack and cannot be overridden by software.
Water Leak - Operating in a marine environment
presents a persistent risk of water entering
electrical enclosures, which could cause shorts or,
in the worst case, battery failure. All electronics
are housed in sealed enclosures with gasketed
cable entries, and IP-rated Deutsch connectors are
used throughout the harness.
HV Bus Short Circuit - A short circuit on the 48
V propulsion bus could result in uncontrolled
current draw, damaging the pack or wiring. Celllevel fusing within the battery pack limits fault
current at the source, and the main contactor
provides a second layer of isolation, allowing the
HV bus to be disconnected immediately in the
event of a detected fault.
Signal Corruption - The motor and Sevcon
switching
waveforms
generate
radiated
interference that could corrupt the motor encoder
signal or CAN bus communications, both of which
are critical to safe motor commutation and control.
Shielded cables with single-point grounding are
used on all critical signal lines to reject this
interference without introducing ground loops.

A. Research & Background

As a first-year entry in the autonomy division,
we designed our software stack with the
philosophy of prioritizing reliability and safety
over potential speed optimizations. We hope to
create a reliable and predictable autonomy system
that can form the foundation of our code for future
years, focusing on optimizing competition
performance during future competitions.
Analyzing the core competition requirements,
we defined three challenges that shaped our
research
process:
reliable
localization,
autonomous path planning, and safe system
behavior.

problem we addressed was localizing our ASV to
understand where our boat was with respect to the
two goal points. Our immediate thought was using
GPS to locate our boat, however, consumer-grade
GPS receivers typically publish fixes at 1–10 Hz
with an accuracy of within three meters.
Unfortunately, this is insufficient for smooth realtime control of a vehicle moving as fast as our
ASV. Thus, to compensate for the GPS’s low
refresh rate, we chose to integrate additional
sensors, notably a six-axis IMU and a
magnetometer, that provided intermediate
information between GPS frames to ensure our
localization algorithm was smooth, continuous,
and accurate.

and more robust reactions to disturbances caused

Ultimately, we determined that an Extended
Kalman Filter (EKF) provided the most accurate
estimation of our boat pose, using IMU readings as
high-rate dead-reckoning updates between GPS
frames, and the magnetometer improving heading
estimation.
2) Path Planning

For autonomous path planning and
motion around the provided waypoints, we
evaluated several guidance strategies. Our
original plan involved implementing a very
common robotic path-following algorithm, Pure
Pursuit, due to its simplicity and widespread use
in ground robotics. Pure Pursuit, provided a
lookahead distance, searches for a point on the
desired path within the lookahead distance and
aims for that point.
However, as outlined in Lekkas and
Fossen (2014), Pure Pursuit simply steers the
vehicle toward a point on the path without
accounting for environmental disturbances that
can occur perpendicular to the track. Known as
cross-track error, it is a common occurrence for
autonomous surface vehicles to be shifted
laterally off their path due to wind and heavy
currents. Thus, ASV's must be able to address a
constant drift that Pure Pursuit simply isn’t suited
to handle.
Lekkas and Fossen suggest an alternative
guidance algorithm, Line-of-Sight (LOS)
navigation, to account for this drift. Rather than
the lookahead distance being a fixed distance

For the path representation itself, we
chose a waypoint-based planner rather than a
map-based path planner such as A*. The
racecourse is an open body of water with no
static obstacles, making the overhead of a full
search-based planner unnecessary. Rather, we
calculate a sparse sequence of waypoints, with
the boat sequentially following waypoint after

circuit can still be triggered, monitoring multiple

B. Framework

We selected ROS 2 (Robot Operating
System 2) as the middleware for our autonomy
stack, providing access to a massive open-source
ecosystem along with tools for building, testing,
and deploying robots. Likewise, its node
architecture allows for splitting features into
individual scripts that can be developed and
tested independently, with communication
systems put into place to allow the easy flow of
data.
C. System Design

The software system is organized as
individual ROS2 nodes, each responsible for a
single function. Nodes communicate via ROS2
topics (ex. sensory data, robot states) and interact
with one another via ROS2 services (ex. discrete
state-change requests).
1) Sensors & Localization
The primary sensors feeding the localization
stack are the ZED-F9P GPS, the ICM-45605 IMU,
and the MMC5983MA magnetometer, all
connected to the Jetson Orin AGX. We utilize the
robot_localization package to run an EKF node,
fusing GPS frames with IMU readings (including
acceleration and gyroscope information), and
magnetometer heading. The output of our EKF is
a smooth odometry estimate that feeds into our
path-planner. Note that we transform all our
locations, including waypoint GPS information,
boat odometry, and target waypoints into a local
frame centered on the first goal point, simplifying
path geometry and calculations.

2) State Management

Our high-level controller implements a state
machine with five states: stationary, manual
control, autonomous control, RC E-stop, and GPS
E-stop. All other nodes subscribe to the state topic
published by this node and use the current state to
determine their behavior. Likewise, we employ a
latching E-stop, preventing further state changes
until the specific fault is resolved.
3) Waypoint Management

At the beginning of the race, our system
calculates a path as an ordered sequence of
waypoints. The system both publishes the current
goal waypoint, as well as constantly calculating the
along-track error between the boat pose and the
next waypoint. If that distance is below a certain
threshold, the system deems that the point has been
reached, switching to the next waypoint. Finally, if
every waypoint is reached, the system determines
that it has completed a lap, adding to a running
total.
4) Line-of-Sight Guidance

The guidance system runs on a timer,
continuously computing a desired heading based
on the ASV’s current position relative to the
planned path. At each step, it calculates the
perpendicular distance from the vessel to the active
path segment (the cross-track error) and applies the
LOS algorithm to steer the vessel toward a
lookahead point ahead of it on the path.

Steering is executed by converting the
desired heading into a physical servo angle,
which is sent over serial to an ESP32 that
computes a PD loop directly on the servo. The
servo controller also has a MUX that selects
between manual and autonomous desired
headings.
Motor control is handled via CANopen to
the Sevcon motor controller. The Sevcon
implements the CiA 402 drive profile, a standard
state machine for electric drives that requires us to
sequence through a specific initialization
procedure (Shutdown, Switch On, Enable
Operation) after which we can send CAN
commands to set the motor torque. Likewise, we
regularly poll motor controller faults and
heartbeat, shutting down the system should the
powertrain not respond as intended.
6) Failsafe
Two independent watchdog processes
protect against loss of critical signals. If no GPS
fix is received within 2 seconds, the system
automatically transitions to a GPS E-stop state
and halts autonomous operation. Similarly, if the
RC receiver reports a sustained loss of signal for
more than 1 second, an RC E-stop is triggered.
Both watchdogs automatically clear and allow the
system to resume once the respective signal is
restored.
V. BUILD PROCESS

Development followed an iterative
process in which each subsystem was tested
independently before integration. Motor control
was validated first on a bench setup, confirming
that the CiA 402 initialization sequence
completed correctly, and that torque commands
produced the expected motor response.

Servo control was tested by commanding
a sweep of angles and verifying that the outboard
was at the correct angle. Likewise, disconnect
failures were tested by deliberately disconnecting
the RC receiver and GPS module and verifying
that the failsafe timeout was activated within the
expected timeframe.
Full system integration was tested in a
Gazebo (VRX) simulation environment, where
the EKF localization, LOS guidance, and
waypoint manager could be exercised together
against a simulated GPS and IMU without
requiring water access.

        Steering is executed by converting the
desired heading into a physical servo angle,
which is sent over serial to an ESP32 that
computes a PD loop directly on the servo. The
servo controller also has a MUX that selects
between manual and autonomous desired
headings.
         Motor control is handled via CANopen to
the Sevcon motor controller. The Sevcon
implements the CiA 402 drive profile, a standard
state machine for electric drives that requires us to
sequence through a specific initialization
procedure (Shutdown, Switch On, Enable
Operation) after which we can send CAN
commands to set the motor torque. Likewise, we
regularly poll motor controller faults and
heartbeat, shutting down the system should the
powertrain not respond as intended.

Manual mode was tested end-to-end with
a live RC controller, confirming that steering and
throttle commands produced the correct servo
and motor responses.
Camera-based obstacle avoidance was prototyped
but is not sufficiently mature for competition use
and will be disabled for the race. This is an
identified area for future development.
VI. SOFTWARE RISKS & MITIGATION

Loss of GPS signal- Without a reliable GPS
frame, localization fails and autonomous guidance
becomes unsafe. Thus, if no GPS fix is received for
more than 2 seconds, the system automatically
halts autonomous operation and holds until the
signal is restored.
Loss of RC signal- The RC controller is the
primary means of operator intervention and
manual E-stop. If contact with the transmitter is
lost for more than 1 second, the system triggers an
estop. A brief grace period prevents spurious
shutdowns from momentary interference, and the
system resumes automatically once the link is reestablished.
Motor Failure- If the software loses the ability to
command the motor, such as due to a CAN bus
fault or software failure, the motor could continue
running at its last commanded torque. Thus, this is
mitigated at the hardware level, with the Sevcon
motor controller being wired into the safety circuit.
Should there be any fault or failure, the motor drive
is independently cut without any software. The
system also checks the drive's fault log on startup
and will not enable the motor if pre-existing faults
are detected.
